screens.title: Replica Set Maintenance and Monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: Maintaining a MongoDB replica set means routine checks, careful configuration changes, and proactive monitoring so your application stays available and consistent. In this lesson you'll learn the practical commands and procedures DBAs use: how to reconfigure members safely, why rolling upgrades protect availability, and how to read rs. status, rs. printReplicationInfo, mongostat and mongotop to find replication lag or resource pressure. We will ground each concept with short examples you can run in mongosh and show a hands-on activity that ties checks and reconfiguration together. This matters because small missteps — like changing a primary without stepping it down or letting oplog windows shrink — can force costly resyncs or create stale reads. You will also see common mistakes and safety steps: back up first, test changes in staging, and set alerts for replication lag and primary status. By the end you should be able to run the core commands, interpret their key fields, plan a rolling upgrade, and take corrective steps when a secondary falls behind. Think about one production system you manage: what alert would you add first to catch replication lag?

screens.title: Reconfiguring a Replica Set
screens.narratorSegment: Reconfiguring a replica set means updating the replica set configuration document that defines members, priorities, and tags. The standard flow is to retrieve the current configuration with rs. conf(), make controlled edits to the members array, and then call rs. reconfig with the modified document. A concrete example is changing a member's priority so it becomes more or less likely to become primary. In the shell you would assign cfg = rs. conf(), then set cfg. members[index]. priority to the new numeric value and call rs. reconfig(cfg). Always make small changes and avoid simultaneously changing multiple critical fields that could trigger an immediate election. A common misconception is that rs. reconfig is harmless; in fact, altering the primary's priority or voting members can force the primary to step down and trigger elections. To reduce risk, prefer changing secondary priorities first and confirm that the replica set has a healthy majority. Another best practice is to capture the current configuration and back it up before applying changes so you can revert if something goes wrong. Key takeaway: rs. reconfig is powerful and must be used deliberately — test the change in staging, back up the config, and monitor rs. status after applying the change to verify member states and optime synchronization. What small change will you make first in a staging replica set?

keyIdea.text: rs.reconfig updates the replica set configuration document; use it for changing priorities, tags, and membership.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Reconfiguring a Replica Set
Definition

Update members, priorities, and tags

Reconfiguration edits the replica set document. This is the authoritative source for member roles and election priorities. Make changes deliberately and validate after applying.

Common example
cfg = rs.conf()
cfg.members[1].priority = 5
rs.reconfig(cfg)
Why it matters
Changing priority affects election behavior and primary availability; done wrong, it can trigger downtime.
Common mistake
Altering voting members or highest-priority member without planning can cause unexpected elections.
Check after reconfig
  • Run rs.status() and confirm each member has health: 1 and the expected stateStr.
  • Verify optimeDate values on secondaries are catching up to the primary.
  • Confirm no unexpected elections occurred and clients remain connected.
Key Takeaway

rs.reconfig edits the source of truth for replica membership. Make incremental changes, back up the config, and verify health after applying.

screens.title: Applying rs.reconfig Safely
screens.narratorSegment: Applying rs. reconfig should be a deliberate, repeatable process. Start by capturing the current configuration with cfg = rs. conf() so you have a known good copy. Inspect members and their priority values to decide which field to change. Make your minimal change, for example adjusting a secondary's priority, and consider lowering or raising values in small increments. Before calling rs. reconfig, ensure a majority of members are healthy and replication lag is low. Call rs. reconfig(cfg) to apply; if the primary's config was altered, MongoDB may initiate a step down and an election. After reconfiguration, run rs. status and rs. printReplicationInfo to validate health, optimeDate parity, and oplog coverage. A common pitfall: changing multiple election-related fields at once or changing voting members can cause instability. Another misconception is that reconfig will auto-fix replication lag — it won't. If secondaries have significant lag, reconfig may make the state worse by causing elections. Always plan to roll back using your saved cfg copy and have a maintenance window. In practice, test your exact cfg changes in staging and automate the check sequence so each reconfig is repeatable and auditable. What pre-checks will you add to your change script?

screens.title: Rolling Upgrade Procedure
screens.narratorSegment: A rolling upgrade is the recommended approach to update MongoDB binaries or underlying OS without causing application downtime. The essential idea is to upgrade members one at a time so a primary remains available. Begin with the secondaries: pick the one with the lowest priority or the one furthest behind if it is safe, shut down the mongod on that secondary, install the new binaries or OS updates, restart mongod and wait for it to catch up and report healthy in rs. status(). Repeat this per secondary until all are upgraded and healthy. Only then step down the primary with rs. stepDown(60) so a newly upgraded secondary can be elected primary. After a new primary is elected, upgrade the old primary (now a secondary), restart it and allow it to rejoin. Finish by verifying every member runs the new version and that replication optimeDates are aligned. A common misconception is that upgrading the primary first is safe; doing so can produce a primary-less period or unexpected elections. Another pitfall is not allowing each restarted member to fully catch up before proceeding, which risks replication lag accumulation. Always verify with rs. printReplicationInfo that the oplog window and optime differences support safe catch-up. The core takeaway: upgrade methodically, verify health between steps, and reserve a maintenance window for unexpected troubleshooting.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Rolling Upgrade Procedure
Overview

Maintain availability while upgrading

  1. Upgrade each secondary one by one: shut down mongod, upgrade, restart, wait for sync.
  2. After secondaries upgraded and healthy, run rs.stepDown(60) on the current primary.
  3. Upgrade the former primary once a new primary is elected and it has transitioned to secondary.
  4. Verify versions and replication health across all members.
Practical checklist
  • Confirm oplog window can support secondary catch-up before you start.
  • Monitor rs.status and optimeDate after each restart and wait until healthy.
  • Keep a maintenance window for unexpected resyncs or slow catch-up.
Key Takeaway

A rolling upgrade keeps a primary available while you update members. Upgrade secondaries first and verify sync before touching the primary.

screens.title: Choosing Which Secondary to Upgrade First
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting the correct secondary to upgrade first reduces risk during a rolling upgrade. Heuristic choices include picking the secondary with the lowest priority or the node that is furthest behind in replication, provided it is safe to do so. If a secondary lags significantly, fixing the cause before applying maintenance is important so you do not propagate or worsen lag across members. Use rs. status() to compare optimeDate values across members and to determine relative replication position. A concrete example: if you have three members and one secondary's optimeDate trails by several minutes, upgrade a different secondary first and investigate the lagging node later to avoid introducing further replication pressure. Avoid the misconception that you should always upgrade the least-used node; usage pattern matters only if it affects replication catch-up. Also, remember that changing the priority of a node before upgrades may influence election preference; plan such changes carefully. Practical steps include recording optimeDate before starting, running mongostat to see current operations per second that may cause lag, and verifying oplog window via rs. printReplicationInfo so the node can catch up after restart. The closing question: what signals will cause you to pause an upgrade and fix replication lag first?

Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Choosing Which Secondary
Heuristic
Lowest priority or healthy, fast-to-sync secondaries first

Use rs.status to compare optimeDate values and choose nodes that will rejoin quickly to avoid extended replication lag during the upgrade process.

Check
optimeDate, health, and oplog window before starting.
Avoid
Starting with a lagging node or changing election-critical fields mid-upgrade.
Example decision flow
  1. Run rs.status() and record optimeDate for each member.
  2. Identify the node with the lowest priority and acceptable lag.
  3. Upgrade it first, wait for catch-up and health, then continue with the next secondary.
Check your understanding

If a node lags, pause and investigate rather than upgrading it first.

screens.title: rs.status() and rs.printReplicationInfo()
screens.narratorSegment: rs. status() and rs. printReplicationInfo() are two essential shell commands for replica set monitoring. rs. status() returns each member's health, state and optime information. The key fields to watch are health (should be 1 for healthy members), stateStr (role such as PRIMARY or SECONDARY), and optimeDate which shows the last applied operation time. Comparing optimeDate values across members reveals replication lag. rs. printReplicationInfo() provides a summary of the Oplog: its size and the time window it covers, which tells you how far back secondaries can catch up without requiring a full resync. For example, a small oplog window means a secondary that goes offline even briefly might not find the needed history to catch up. A common misconception is checking only member states and ignoring the oplog; both matter because health without a sufficient oplog window still risks needing a full resync after downtime. When you run these commands in mongosh, note optimeDate timestamps and compare them numerically or by elapsed time to measure lag. As a practical step, capture rs. status() before and after maintenance to validate no members lost health. Closing question: when you see a secondary with recent optimeDate far behind the primary, what immediate steps will you take to diagnose the cause?

Command

rs.status()

Look for health: 1, stateStr indicating role, and optimeDate to compare replication position across members.

screens.title: Using mongostat and mongotop for Real-Time Monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: mongostat and mongotop are lightweight command-line utilities that give you immediate visibility into a running mongod instance. mongostat reports operations per second like inserts, queries, updates and deletes, as well as memory and page fault metrics. Use mongostat --port 27017 to watch short-term spikes during maintenance or load tests. mongotop shows read and write activity per collection, helping you identify hot collections that may cause heavy disk input and output and slow replication. A concrete example from the chapter: open one terminal and run mongostat --port 27017, open another and run mongotop --port 27017, then perform a small script of inserts and queries in mongosh to see the changes reflected in both tools. Interpreting the output requires context: a spike in inserts with correlated high page faults or disk write latency indicates potential input and output bottlenecks you should investigate. A common misconception is that these tools replace detailed monitoring systems; they are quick diagnostics, not long-term metrics stores. During upgrades, use mongostat to ensure operations per second remain stable and mongotop to confirm that collections rebuild or repair activity is not overwhelming disk. The takeaway: these utilities are your fast feedback loop during maintenance. When you see unusual values, pause and use db. currentOp and rs. status for deeper diagnosis.

screens.title: Key Metrics to Monitor
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring the right metrics helps you catch problems before they affect clients. Replication lag is the time difference between the primary's optime and a secondary's optime; persistent high lag means secondaries return outdated data to any reads directed there and can indicate network or resource bottlenecks. The oplog window shows how much history is retained: a too-small oplog can force a full resync if a secondary falls behind. Connection count tells you how many open connections each mongod has — sudden increases can point to client issues or connection leaks. C P U, memory, and disk input and output are essential system-level metrics: MongoDB is often input and output sensitive, so watch disk latency and throughput during heavy writes. Finally, operations per second (inserts, queries, updates, deletes) reveals workload patterns; spikes might require capacity planning or throttling during maintenance. A common mistake is monitoring only one class of metrics — for example, looking at C P U but ignoring replication lag or oplog size. Effective monitoring combines replication position, oplog window, and system metrics and ties them to alerts. For instance, an alert for sustained replication lag plus rising disk write latency should trigger investigation before a secondary falls out of the oplog window. The takeaway: instrument all relevant signals and correlate them to make informed maintenance decisions.

Replication Lag
Compare optimeDate across members

Oplog Window

Connections & Ops/sec
Track client connections and operation rates

System Resources
CPU, memory, disk I/O

Correlate metrics

screens.title: Common Maintenance Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: Maintenance carries risk when procedures are not followed. The chapter lists common mistakes: shutting down a primary without stepping it down, ignoring replication lag, under-provisioning the oplog, and lacking alerting. Shutting down the primary abruptly can trigger an unplanned failover and disrupt client traffic. The immediate operational concern from persistent replication lag is that reads from a lagging secondary will be outdated, which creates inconsistency for applications using secondary reads. Under-sized oplogs force full resyncs for secondaries that fall too far behind, which is expensive and slow. Finally, relying only on manual checks without alerting means problems are discovered too late. Safety notes summarize how to mitigate these risks: always back up data before major maintenance, test procedures in staging, ensure the oplog window supports your expected offline times, and implement automated alerts for primary status and replication lag. A practical habit is to run a short pre-maintenance checklist: capture rs. status and rs. printReplicationInfo, ensure oplog and health are sufficient, start mongostat and mongotop monitors, then perform changes. If anything deviates, pause and diagnose rather than continue. The takeaway: treat maintenance as a repeatable, scripted procedure with checkpoints and alerts so mistakes become rare and reversible.

fullNarratorScript:
Maintaining a MongoDB replica set means routine checks, careful configuration changes, and proactive monitoring so your application stays available and consistent. In this lesson you'll learn the practical commands and procedures DBAs use: how to reconfigure members safely, why rolling upgrades protect availability, and how to read rs. status, rs. printReplicationInfo, mongostat and mongotop to find replication lag or resource pressure. We will ground each concept with short examples you can run in mongosh and show a hands-on activity that ties checks and reconfiguration together. This matters because small missteps — like changing a primary without stepping it down or letting oplog windows shrink — can force costly resyncs or create stale reads. You will also see common mistakes and safety steps: back up first, test changes in staging, and set alerts for replication lag and primary status. By the end you should be able to run the core commands, interpret their key fields, plan a rolling upgrade, and take corrective steps when a secondary falls behind. Think about one production system you manage: what alert would you add first to catch replication lag?

These objectives focus your practice on the precise operations and checks a DBA must run to keep replica sets healthy. You will perform common maintenance tasks such as reconfiguring members and changing priorities. You will also explain and execute a rolling upgrade sequence that preserves availability by upgrading secondaries before the primary. We will practice the essential shell commands you need to check replica set health and replication windows. Finally, you will identify the key metrics to monitor and learn how to interpret them so you can detect replication lag, oplog pressure, or resource exhaustion before they affect your application. Each objective links a practical skill with why it matters: reconfiguration prevents unexpected elections when done carefully, rolling upgrades avoid downtime, monitoring commands let you spot lag, and metrics guide alerting and capacity planning. By the end, you should be able to perform these tasks in a staging environment and choose the first alert you would create for production.

These objectives emphasize not only how to run commands but what to prioritize in production. You will be able to interpret rs. printReplicationInfo to assess oplog window size and understand why an undersized oplog can force expensive resyncs. You will also learn to read db. currentOp to spot long-running operations that may slow replication or cause high input and output. Finally, you will prioritize metrics for alerting: replication lag first, then primary status, oplog window, and resource metrics. The outcome is a checklist you can apply immediately: run rs. status to confirm health, verify the oplog window is sufficient, use mongostat and mongotop to identify hotspots, then schedule maintenance using a rolling upgrade sequence. This objective set reduces risk by tying each command to an operational consequence and a monitoring action you can automate. As you practice, ask: which metric would trigger an automated failover alert in your environment?

Reconfiguring a replica set means updating the replica set configuration document that defines members, priorities, and tags. The standard flow is to retrieve the current configuration with rs. conf(), make controlled edits to the members array, and then call rs. reconfig with the modified document. A concrete example is changing a member's priority so it becomes more or less likely to become primary. In the shell you would assign cfg = rs. conf(), then set cfg. members[index]. priority to the new numeric value and call rs. reconfig(cfg). Always make small changes and avoid simultaneously changing multiple critical fields that could trigger an immediate election. A common misconception is that rs. reconfig is harmless; in fact, altering the primary's priority or voting members can force the primary to step down and trigger elections. To reduce risk, prefer changing secondary priorities first and confirm that the replica set has a healthy majority. Another best practice is to capture the current configuration and back it up before applying changes so you can revert if something goes wrong. Key takeaway: rs. reconfig is powerful and must be used deliberately — test the change in staging, back up the config, and monitor rs. status after applying the change to verify member states and optime synchronization. What small change will you make first in a staging replica set?

Applying rs. reconfig should be a deliberate, repeatable process. Start by capturing the current configuration with cfg = rs. conf() so you have a known good copy. Inspect members and their priority values to decide which field to change. Make your minimal change, for example adjusting a secondary's priority, and consider lowering or raising values in small increments. Before calling rs. reconfig, ensure a majority of members are healthy and replication lag is low. Call rs. reconfig(cfg) to apply; if the primary's config was altered, MongoDB may initiate a step down and an election. After reconfiguration, run rs. status and rs. printReplicationInfo to validate health, optimeDate parity, and oplog coverage. A common pitfall: changing multiple election-related fields at once or changing voting members can cause instability. Another misconception is that reconfig will auto-fix replication lag — it won't. If secondaries have significant lag, reconfig may make the state worse by causing elections. Always plan to roll back using your saved cfg copy and have a maintenance window. In practice, test your exact cfg changes in staging and automate the check sequence so each reconfig is repeatable and auditable. What pre-checks will you add to your change script?

A rolling upgrade is the recommended approach to update MongoDB binaries or underlying OS without causing application downtime. The essential idea is to upgrade members one at a time so a primary remains available. Begin with the secondaries: pick the one with the lowest priority or the one furthest behind if it is safe, shut down the mongod on that secondary, install the new binaries or OS updates, restart mongod and wait for it to catch up and report healthy in rs. status(). Repeat this per secondary until all are upgraded and healthy. Only then step down the primary with rs. stepDown(60) so a newly upgraded secondary can be elected primary. After a new primary is elected, upgrade the old primary (now a secondary), restart it and allow it to rejoin. Finish by verifying every member runs the new version and that replication optimeDates are aligned. A common misconception is that upgrading the primary first is safe; doing so can produce a primary-less period or unexpected elections. Another pitfall is not allowing each restarted member to fully catch up before proceeding, which risks replication lag accumulation. Always verify with rs. printReplicationInfo that the oplog window and optime differences support safe catch-up. The core takeaway: upgrade methodically, verify health between steps, and reserve a maintenance window for unexpected troubleshooting.

Selecting the correct secondary to upgrade first reduces risk during a rolling upgrade. Heuristic choices include picking the secondary with the lowest priority or the node that is furthest behind in replication, provided it is safe to do so. If a secondary lags significantly, fixing the cause before applying maintenance is important so you do not propagate or worsen lag across members. Use rs. status() to compare optimeDate values across members and to determine relative replication position. A concrete example: if you have three members and one secondary's optimeDate trails by several minutes, upgrade a different secondary first and investigate the lagging node later to avoid introducing further replication pressure. Avoid the misconception that you should always upgrade the least-used node; usage pattern matters only if it affects replication catch-up. Also, remember that changing the priority of a node before upgrades may influence election preference; plan such changes carefully. Practical steps include recording optimeDate before starting, running mongostat to see current operations per second that may cause lag, and verifying oplog window via rs. printReplicationInfo so the node can catch up after restart. The closing question: what signals will cause you to pause an upgrade and fix replication lag first?

rs. status() and rs. printReplicationInfo() are two essential shell commands for replica set monitoring. rs. status() returns each member's health, state and optime information. The key fields to watch are health (should be 1 for healthy members), stateStr (role such as PRIMARY or SECONDARY), and optimeDate which shows the last applied operation time. Comparing optimeDate values across members reveals replication lag. rs. printReplicationInfo() provides a summary of the Oplog: its size and the time window it covers, which tells you how far back secondaries can catch up without requiring a full resync. For example, a small oplog window means a secondary that goes offline even briefly might not find the needed history to catch up. A common misconception is checking only member states and ignoring the oplog; both matter because health without a sufficient oplog window still risks needing a full resync after downtime. When you run these commands in mongosh, note optimeDate timestamps and compare them numerically or by elapsed time to measure lag. As a practical step, capture rs. status() before and after maintenance to validate no members lost health. Closing question: when you see a secondary with recent optimeDate far behind the primary, what immediate steps will you take to diagnose the cause?

mongostat and mongotop are lightweight command-line utilities that give you immediate visibility into a running mongod instance. mongostat reports operations per second like inserts, queries, updates and deletes, as well as memory and page fault metrics. Use mongostat --port 27017 to watch short-term spikes during maintenance or load tests. mongotop shows read and write activity per collection, helping you identify hot collections that may cause heavy disk input and output and slow replication. A concrete example from the chapter: open one terminal and run mongostat --port 27017, open another and run mongotop --port 27017, then perform a small script of inserts and queries in mongosh to see the changes reflected in both tools. Interpreting the output requires context: a spike in inserts with correlated high page faults or disk write latency indicates potential input and output bottlenecks you should investigate. A common misconception is that these tools replace detailed monitoring systems; they are quick diagnostics, not long-term metrics stores. During upgrades, use mongostat to ensure operations per second remain stable and mongotop to confirm that collections rebuild or repair activity is not overwhelming disk. The takeaway: these utilities are your fast feedback loop during maintenance. When you see unusual values, pause and use db. currentOp and rs. status for deeper diagnosis.

Monitoring the right metrics helps you catch problems before they affect clients. Replication lag is the time difference between the primary's optime and a secondary's optime; persistent high lag means secondaries return outdated data to any reads directed there and can indicate network or resource bottlenecks. The oplog window shows how much history is retained: a too-small oplog can force a full resync if a secondary falls behind. Connection count tells you how many open connections each mongod has — sudden increases can point to client issues or connection leaks. C P U, memory, and disk input and output are essential system-level metrics: MongoDB is often input and output sensitive, so watch disk latency and throughput during heavy writes. Finally, operations per second (inserts, queries, updates, deletes) reveals workload patterns; spikes might require capacity planning or throttling during maintenance. A common mistake is monitoring only one class of metrics — for example, looking at C P U but ignoring replication lag or oplog size. Effective monitoring combines replication position, oplog window, and system metrics and ties them to alerts. For instance, an alert for sustained replication lag plus rising disk write latency should trigger investigation before a secondary falls out of the oplog window. The takeaway: instrument all relevant signals and correlate them to make informed maintenance decisions.
